newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Kiguel challenges rating agencies.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Kiguel challenges rating agencies.

text.p: Undersecretary of Finance Miguel Kiguel Tuesday challenged the view of Argentina held by credit rating agencies, arguing that, in many ways, the country has better credentials than some investment-grade countries.

"The progress observed in the economic indicators in the 1990s still have not been reflected fully in improvements in Argentina's credit rating by the rating agencies," Kiguel told a banking conference in Buenos Aires. He based his argument on a comparison between Argentina and the economic indicators of countries with the lowest investment-grade ratings.
Argentina is rated BB by Standard & Poor's, two notches below investment grade. BBB is the lowest investment-grade rating.

Kiguel listed gross domestic product, income per capita, growth, inflation, budget deficits, debt as a proportion of GDP, debt as a proportion of exports, current account deficits and international reserves as a proportion of imports for his comparison.
Of these, Argentina's performance is actually stronger on seven of the eight than the average of BBB-rated countries.
The only area where Argentina scored less was the debt proportion of exports. Argentina's debt represents 283 percent of exports compared with an average 146 percent for BBB-rated countries.

GDP per capita income in Argentina is $8,666 compared with an average $4,981 for BBB countries. Argentina's inflation is 0.1 percent and 19.2 percent for BBB rated nations. The figures are based on a Goldman Sachs report.

Kiguel added that the measurement of Argentina's total and external debt levels is actually wrong in some ways. For one, he pointed out that many rating agencies do not consider the amount of Argentine dollar debt held by Argentines.

"Some analysts confuse debt denominated in dollars with foreign debt, without distinguishing if the lender is an Argentine resident or foreigner," said Kiguel. If measured this way, Argentina's foreign debt is $67 billion rather than $88 billion.

Another point is Argentina's purchase of zero-coupon U.S. Treasury notes as guarantees for its Brady debt. The value of these at maturity should be netted out into the country's total debt burden. Total debt would then fall by $15.8 billion.

Kiguel recognized many economic challenges lie in Argentina's path to investment-grade status. But he pointed out that S&P's recent decision to raise some Argentine corporations and banks above the sovereign rating ceiling to BBB- was a vote of confidence.
"It would be difficult to give an investment-grade rating if S&P did not expect continuity in macro-economic stability and current economic policy," he said.
